findings.title: The friction histogram's top row is the pull-request trailers, not friction
findings.claim: Over the window the production friction histogram's largest row, `(unlabelled friction bullet)` at 13 distinct pull requests of 54 (24 %) and 13 of 66 entries (19.7 %), is 13 pull-request trailer lines (`🤖 Generated with [Claude Code]` x11, `Co-Authored-By: …` x1, `Closes #1134` x1) that fall inside the `## Friction` section because a body's trailers follow its last heading, and it clears the threshold of 3, so the filer proposes `would open "[policy] recurring friction: (unlabelled friction bullet)"`.
findings.mechanism: `policy_lint.mjs:sections` ends a section at the next `^## ` heading, and a body's trailers sit after the last section, so they are inside `## Friction`; `frictionEntries` keeps a section's first line as an entry whenever no bullet opens one (`if (opens || !lines.length) lines.push(raw)`); that entry has no id, and `frictionIds` maps a null id to FRICTION_UNLABELLED. The bucket is therefore positional: `--perturb trailer-out` takes one trailer out of one section and `friction_entries` does not move (66 -> 66) because the next tail line is promoted into the same bucket.

evidence.unit: trailer entries in the (unlabelled friction bullet) key
evidence.machine: any (network-bound counts and a Node subprocess)
evidence.contention_note: fan-out box shared with other auditors; counts only, no timing

perturbation.change: `--perturb trailer-out`: insert a `## Trailers` heading before one body's trailer line, taking it out of the section the parser reads (fixture edit in memory; no live pull request touched)
perturbation.observed_value: trailer_entries 13 -> 12; friction_entries 66 -> 66 (the bucket is positional, so unlabelled_entries stays 13)

findings.metric_definition: Entries the production friction parser returns that are pull-request trailer lines, and the share of the window's friction entries they are.

null_control.value: every per-file count unchanged (62 of 66 entries unaffected; one-file 43, several 0)
null_control.note: re-spelling an id changes the string, not the file, so a count that moved here would show the harness reading spelling rather than the rule

reproduction_steps: cd <repository root>; PYTHONPATH=tests/hastub python3 /tmp/heatpump-orch/audit-r5-D13/h6_friction.py  # prints each trailer with its PR number

cross-check: GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node .claude/workflows/policy_lint.mjs --stats --since 34efcbae0d32f8dc4a28cf959412c349b5587829  # prints `13 / 13 (unlabelled friction bullet) <- at or over threshold` and `would open`
findings.proposed_fix_scope: In `frictionEntries`, require a bullet/`<id>: <class>:` shape (or stop the section at the body's first trailer line) rather than admitting a section's first arbitrary line; one function, no policy text.

findings.title: 16 of the window's 30 blocked verdicts are outside the wave's own grammar
findings.claim: Of the 86 `Fix review:` lines the window contains, 18 (20.9 %) do not match web-fix-wave.js:VERDICT_RE; among the 30 blocked-shaped ones, 7 are the bare `Fix review: blocked` (no SHA, no class, no reason on the line parseVerdict reads) and 9 carry a class word VERDICT_CLASSES does not have (body-only x2, claim-contradiction, regression, stale-ownership, unseen-write-failure, missing-id-unload, carry-unfaithful, remedy), so 16 of 30 blocked rounds have no route to a repair -- and first-pass yield is 0.593 under the brief's prefix rule against 0.722 under VERDICT_RE, a 13-point swing caused by exactly those items.
findings.mechanism: `parseVerdict` reads only the comment's first line (`raw = comment.split('\n')[0]`) and throws on anything VERDICT_RE refuses; the wave prompt states that a blocked verdict without a class 'is unreadable and is treated as blocked with no route to a repair'. The reviewers wrote their reason from line 2 on (all 7 bare ones do), or used a class word the grammar's eleven do not include.

evidence.contention_note: fan-out box shared with other auditors; counts only

perturbation.change: `--perturb classes`: the nine class words the window's reviewers wrote, appended to VERDICT_CLASSES in a copy of web-fix-wave.js under the temp root

findings.metric_definition: Share of `Fix review:` first lines that the production VERDICT_RE refuses, and of blocked-shaped lines whose class word is absent from VERDICT_CLASSES.

null_control.note: the opposite edit (`\s+` -> `\s\s+`) must take the parsed count to zero; it does

leave_one_out.note: cells are the eleven VERDICT_CLASSES plus the outside-grammar row; the outside row alone (16) exceeds every grammar class, and dropping nothing changes the claim because the count is a partition

reproduction_steps: cd <repository root>; PYTHONPATH=tests/hastub python3 /tmp/heatpump-orch/audit-r5-D13/h1_verdicts.py  # prints every blocked-shaped line with its written class word
findings.proposed_fix_scope: Either widen VERDICT_CLASSES to the words reviewers use and require the reason on the first line, or make parseVerdict fall back to a defined class (with the raw line recorded) instead of throwing; both are the grammar's side, not a new check.

findings.title: The window-level verdict histogram can emit one key, and its own note says otherwise
findings.claim: Run over the window, `policy_lint.mjs --stats` prints `verdict grammar ["blocked","merge"] read from .claude/workflows/web-fix-wave.js` and emits zero block-class rows over a window containing 30 blocked verdicts, because VERDICT_LITERAL_RE scans for string literals while the wave script names all eleven VERDICT_CLASSES by interpolating ${VERDICT_CLASSES.join(', ')} and places the class after the head SHA; spelling the eleven words out in that prompt is a null control (the printed grammar stays at 2), so the exclusion the instrument's comment calls conditional ('a third verdict class ... makes this arm informative again') is permanent.
findings.mechanism: `verdictClasses()` extracts `"Fix review:\s+([a-z]+)` from the wave script's source; the wave script teaches merge and blocked as literals and the class vocabulary as an interpolation that no literal scan can see. The histogram regex `^Fix review:\s*(class)\b` then keys on the word after `Fix review:`, which is always merge or blocked.

evidence.unit: block-class rows emitted by the histogram over 30 blocked verdicts
evidence.machine: any (runs the production CLI in a baseline worktree)
evidence.contention_note: fan-out box shared with other auditors; counts only

perturbation.change: `--perturb verdict-word`: one more literal `"Fix review: fold ${sha}"` added to the reviewer prompt of a web-fix-wave.js copy inside a baseline worktree

findings.metric_definition: Distinct verdict words the production --stats mode reports it read from the wave script, and distinct block-class rows its histogram prints.

null_control.note: spelling all eleven classes out in the prompt -- the change the instrument's own comment says would make its arm informative -- does not move the number, so the arm is excluded permanently while reading as excluded conditionally

findings.proposed_fix_scope: Read the class vocabulary from VERDICT_CLASSES (the declaration, as h1_grammar.mjs already does) and key the histogram on the class that follows the SHA, or drop the arm and say the histogram cannot count block classes.

findings.title: The carried governance set understates governance cost by 7 %
findings.claim: round4/D11/governance_cost.py:GOV names `record-status`, a job in no workflow file at this baseline, and omits `delivery-status` and `delivery-status-publish`, which governance.yml defines; re-derived from the workflow files at the baseline, governance_share at the pull-request head is 0.0556 where the carried set gives 0.0515 on the same 54 merges (169 s vs 157 s of governance seconds per merge, 7.4 % relative understatement).
findings.mechanism: The set is a literal in the harness rather than a derivation from the workflow files, so renaming a job (record-status -> delivery-status / delivery-status-publish) leaves the harness naming a job that does not exist and missing the seconds of the ones that do. Nothing makes the number fail; it silently reports a smaller share.

evidence.unit: governance share of CI seconds per merge at the pull-request head (carried set: 0.0515)
evidence.contention_note: durations are GitHub's own, contention-immune; no wall clock on this box is read

perturbation.change: `--gov briefs-drop`: one job removed from the derived governance set, the value the number is keyed on

findings.metric_definition: Governance job seconds divided by all check-run seconds at the same head, per merge, with the governance set derived from the workflow files.

null_control.note: round 4's carried set on the same population: lower, and the difference is the two governance jobs it does not name

leave_one_out.note: cells are the 54 merges; the share with the most governance-heavy merge dropped is 0.0532 against 0.0556, so the figure is not carried by one merge

findings.proposed_fix_scope: Derive GOV from the workflow files (jobs in governance.yml plus jobs whose run: blocks invoke .claude/workflows/) instead of carrying a literal set.

could_not_finish: `--stats` takes a ref, not a timestamp, so h7 reaches the window through the parent of the window's oldest first-parent commit; the two enumerators agree (54 merges) but are different code paths.
There is no single per-merge population for CI seconds: the pre-merge gate and the post-merge push run are different rounds at different costs, so h5 prints both and a judge must pick one.
time-to-restore has one episode in the whole window (delivery-status-publish cancelled x3), so h4's TTR table is one row and is not evidence about the loop's recovery time.
